decisions.quote: Experimental Economics Replication Project Replication of Expectations as Endowments: Evidence on Reference-Dependent Preferences from Exchange and Valuation Experiments by Ericson, K.M.M./Fuster, A. (2011) in: The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 126(4), pp. 1879–1907. Replication Authors: Adam Altmejd, Anna Dreber, Emma Heikensten and Magnus Johannesson In a valuation experiment, Marzilli Ericson and Fuster randomize subjects to a high or low probability of obtaining an item (a mug) and elicit their willingness-to-accept it. They find that the high probability treatment increases the valuation of the item. The paper includes two experiments where other things are also tested. Experiment 2 was chosen as it was the last experiment.
decisions.location: Primary Project Replication Report for Ericson and Fuster (2011), header and introduction (line 1312); see also Reference 41 (lines 302-304) and Table S2 (lines 1169-1174)
decisions.reason: The primary replication report, Reference 41, Table S1, and Table S2 explicitly identify Ericson and Fuster (2011), 'Expectations as Endowments: Evidence on Reference-Dependent Preferences from Exchange and Valuation Experiments' (QJE 126(4): 1879-1907, Experiment 2), as the original study re-tested in this replication. Both the shipped record and blind target 8 identify this same original paper.

decisions.quote: Discussion Given the criteria and procedure outlined above, the hypothesis of interest has not been replicated at a significance level of α < 5%. The relative effect size equals 68.75% and the p-value of the hypothesis test is p = 0.055. However, it is a borderline case. The p-value is slightly above 0.05. If the tests are carried out directly comparing the mean W T A between the two treatments (with or without a log transformation) without deducting the W T A of the pen, the p-value is < 0.05 (but this test was not significant in the original study).
decisions.location: Primary Project Replication Report for Ericson and Fuster (2011), Discussion section (line 1312); see also Replication Results (line 1312) and Table S1 (line 1263)
decisions.reason: In the individual primary replication report for Ericson and Fuster (2011), the authors explicitly state the overall verdict that 'the original result is thus not replicated' and 'the hypothesis of interest has not been replicated at a significance level of α < 5%' (p = 0.055 vs. original p = 0.030; Table S1 Replicated = No). Under Codebook Rule 1, the authors' explicit overall verdict on the focal tested hypothesis governs over exploratory/alternative specifications that were not significant in the original study.

decisions.quote: The original sample size is 112 participants (52 in the mh treatment and 60 in the ml treatment). To achieve 90% power the required sample size is 250 participants. The sample for replication consists of 250 students from Harvard University (their Harvard IDs will be checked).
decisions.location: Primary Project Replication Report for Ericson and Fuster (2011), Power Analysis and Sample sections (line 1312)
decisions.reason: The study collected new experimental data from a fresh sample of Harvard University students (262 actual participants) to re-test the published finding from Experiment 2 of Ericson and Fuster (2011), which makes it a replication.

decisions.location: Supplementary Materials, Section 1. Replications (lines 606-610); see also Reference 50 (lines 320-321), Table S2 (lines 1206-1211), and Table S1 (line 1272)
decisions.reason: Supplementary Section 1, Reference 50 ('I. Kuziemko, R. W. Buell, T. Reich, M. I. Norton, “Last-place aversion”: Ev-idence and redistributive implications, Q. J. Econ. 129, 105 (2014)'), Table S1, and Table S2 explicitly identify Kuziemko et al. (2014) as one of the 18 original studies replicated in this project. Both the shipped record and blind target 17 identify this same original paper.

decisions.location: Supplementary Materials, Table S1. Replication results (lines 1253-1272)
decisions.reason: Although the separate individual replication report for Kuziemko et al. (2014) is not appended to the source text, Table S1 of the main paper's supplementary materials explicitly attributes the replication outcome to Kuziemko et al. (QJE 2014, Ref. 50): Original P-value = 0.070, Original Effect Size (r) = 0.28, Original N = 42, Replication P-value = 0.154, Replication Effect Size (r) = -0.12 (in the opposite direction to the original), Replication N = 144, Replicated = No, Relative Effect Size (r) = -0.42 (-0.39). This explicit per-study author verdict in Table S1 establishes that the replication failed.

decisions.quote:
1. Replications
We replicate 18 experimental studies published between 2011 and 2014 in the high-
impact general interest journals the American Economic Review (AER) and the Quarterly
Journal of Economics (QJE). (33–50) The deadline for inclusion in the study was that the
paper should be published or posted as accepted/in press at the website of the journal at
August 1, 2014.
decisions.location: Supplementary Materials, Section 1. Replications (lines 557-562); see also Table S1 (line 1272)
decisions.reason: The authors conducted a new laboratory experiment with a fresh sample of N = 144 participants (compared to N = 42 in the original study, as shown in Table S1) to re-test the finding of Kuziemko et al. (2014, Ref. 50), making this a replication.
